summary: This RFC proposes another subnet addressing scheme that in most cases needs no change to host software. The drawbacks are that the number of subnets per network is limited and all gateways need modification.

eli5.summary: A way to split a network into smaller parts so ordinary computers need no changes, though only routers must learn the trick.

questions: what is the subnetwork addressing scheme in rfc 932
subtitle: A way to split one IP network into multiple subnets without changing host software.

tldr.problem: Networks wanted to divide themselves into subnets for internal routing efficiency, but making hosts aware of subnets required modifying all host software, which was impractical for deployed systems.
tldr.mechanism: Assign subnet numbers using Class C addresses with a high-order bit set to distinguish them, so distant routers can collapse multiple subnets into one entry by ignoring the third byte (a "Class B 1/2" address). Hosts see only regular Class C addresses and require no changes.
tldr.outcome: The scheme limited each network to 256 subnets maximum and required all routers to be updated, so it saw mixed adoption. Mogul's RFC 917 (variable-length subnet mask) became more popular.

facts.label: Subnet distinguished by
facts.value: Third byte of reserved Class C address

facts.label: Router changes required
facts.value: All routers must implement Class B 1/2 logic

today: RFC 932 is an historic proposal for subnetting. The Internet adopted RFC 917's variable-length subnet mask approach instead, which became known as CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) and is standard today. RFC 932 showed the problem was solvable but not the final solution.

sections.title: The Subnet Problem
sections.content:
Subnets are logical divisions of a network, used to group hosts by physical location or administrative boundary. Without subnets, a large network must allocate a new network number each time it adds a cable, wasting address space. With subnets, one network number can cover many internal segments.

RFC 917 (Mogul) proposed one approach: encode the subnet number in the host part of the address so hosts and routers could extract it. But this required modifying every host to understand the encoding—a practical barrier when thousands of systems were already deployed.

RFC 932 asks: can we add subnets while leaving all host software unchanged?
sections.eli5: A company has 10 office buildings but only one main address. How do you sort mail between buildings without retaining mail carriers everywhere?

sections.title: The Addressing Scheme
sections.content:
The proposal reserves the upper half of Class C address space (those with the high-order bit set) for subnet use. When a network wants to use subnets, it claims a contiguous block of 256 such Class C addresses. Each address in that block becomes a subnet, distinguished by the third byte.

Hosts on that subnetted network treat addresses as ordinary Class C and require zero modification. A distant router, upon seeing a reserved Class C address (high bit set), checks whether it is directly attached to that network. If not, it ignores the third byte and treats the first two bytes as a Class B 1/2 address—collapsing all 256 subnets into one routing entry.
sections.eli5: Each building gets its own mailbox number (the third byte), but from the outside, all buildings share one main number. Distant post offices only need to know the main number.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.content:
The scheme has two major drawbacks. First, it limits each network to 256 subnets maximum; a larger network must claim multiple blocks and accept them as separate networks internally. Second, all routers must understand the Class B 1/2 encoding, making it a mandatory, coordinated change across the Internet.

RFC 917's variable-length subnet mask (adopted later) proved more flexible, allowing different networks to choose different subnet depths and avoiding the 256-subnet cap. As a result, RFC 932 saw limited real-world adoption, though it demonstrated the feasibility of transparent subnetting.
sections.eli5: The trick worked but was hard to roll out everywhere, and other ideas turned out to be more flexible.
